title: Emergency and Critical Care
tagline: The ABCDE approach, resuscitation, shock, airway and ventilation, poisoning, anaphylaxis, intensive care and major incidents
summary: Emergencies leave little time to think, so they are managed with structured approaches. This course covers the assessment of the acutely ill patient, cardiac arrest and resuscitation, shock and fluid therapy, airway and ventilation, poisoning, anaphylaxis and acute asthma, the care of critically ill patients, and triage in major incidents.
overview: Emergency and critical care medicine is applied physiology under time pressure. An acutely ill patient rarely arrives with a diagnosis, so the clinician must first find and reverse whatever threatens the airway, breathing, circulation or brain, in the order in which those failures kill, and only then work out the cause. This course teaches that structured approach and the specific emergencies that fill a resuscitation room and an acute medical take.

It begins with the ABCDE assessment, early-warning scores and escalation, then covers cardiac arrest and the peri-arrest rhythms, shock and intravenous fluids, the airway, oxygen therapy and mechanical ventilation, poisoning, and anaphylaxis with acute severe asthma. The later chapters move to the intensive care unit, where organs are supported for days or weeks and the complications of treatment must be prevented, and to major incidents, where the same logic is applied to many patients at once.

The course uses numbers where they help decisions: NEWS2 scores, oxygen delivery, the A–a gradient, predicted body weight and driving pressure, the anion and osmolar gaps, the paracetamol treatment line, SOFA scores and triage counts. UK guidance is followed (Resuscitation Council UK, NICE, the British Thoracic Society, the Difficult Airway Society, NHS England), with the dates of the versions used. Doses appear only as the standard adult values printed in those guidelines, for teaching; practice follows current local guidance.
outcomes: Perform a structured ABCDE assessment of an acutely unwell adult, calculate and act on a NEWS2 score, and escalate clearly using SBAR.

Explain why chest compressions work, apply the Resuscitation Council UK adult ALS algorithm including drug timing in shockable and non-shockable rhythms, and search for the reversible causes of cardiac arrest.
Manage peri-arrest bradycardia and tachycardia by recognising adverse features, and outline the targets of post-resuscitation care and the principles of decisions about CPR.

Classify shock as hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive or obstructive, calculate oxygen delivery, and reason about fluid responsiveness, choice of fluid, vasopressors and the management of major haemorrhage.
Assess and manage the airway, follow the Difficult Airway Society plan for failed intubation, prescribe oxygen to a target, and interpret respiratory failure with the A–a gradient.
Describe the indications for CPAP and non-invasive ventilation, and the principles of lung-protective mechanical ventilation and prone positioning in ARDS.

Recognise poisoning by toxidrome and investigation, apply decontamination and enhanced elimination appropriately, interpret the UK paracetamol treatment line, and describe the specific treatment of common serious poisonings and the care of the person who has self-harmed.
Recognise anaphylaxis and its mimics, outline its emergency treatment and follow-up according to UK guidance, distinguish bradykinin-mediated angio-oedema, and grade acute asthma.

Describe the organisation of critical care, sepsis and the SOFA score, sedation and delirium, weaning, nutrition, prevention of ICU-acquired complications, communication with families and recovery after critical illness.
Apply UK major incident structures (METHANE, command levels, JESIP) and mass-casualty triage, and discuss the ethics of allocating care when resources are overwhelmed.

history.title: Anaphylaxis described
history.detail: Charles Richet and Paul Portier find that dogs given a second small dose of a sea anemone toxin, weeks after a first, collapse and die within minutes. They name the phenomenon anaphylaxis, 'against protection'. Richet received the Nobel Prize in 1913.

history.title: Defibrillation of the exposed heart
history.detail: Claude Beck, a surgeon in Cleveland, restores a perfusing rhythm in a teenage boy who developed ventricular fibrillation during chest surgery, by applying a shock directly to the heart: the first successful human defibrillation.

history.title: Polio and the first intensive care unit
history.detail: During the Copenhagen poliomyelitis epidemic, the anaesthetist Bjørn Ibsen treats respiratory paralysis with tracheostomy and manual positive-pressure ventilation, delivered around the clock by medical students. Mortality falls sharply, and grouping such patients together becomes the model for intensive care.

history.title: Closed-chest cardiac massage
history.detail: William Kouwenhoven, James Jude and Guy Knickerbocker at Johns Hopkins report that rhythmic external chest compression can maintain circulation in cardiac arrest. Combined with the mouth-to-mouth ventilation championed by Peter Safar and James Elam, it becomes cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

history.title: Direct-current defibrillation and cardioversion
history.detail: Bernard Lown and colleagues in Boston introduce the direct-current defibrillator and the synchronised shock, making cardioversion of arrhythmias safe and defibrillation more effective.

history.title: The mobile coronary care unit
history.detail: Frank Pantridge and John Geddes in Belfast equip an ambulance with a portable defibrillator and send it to patients with suspected heart attacks, showing that defibrillation can be brought to the patient before hospital.

history.title: International resuscitation guidelines and lung-protective ventilation
history.detail: The International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (founded 1992) publishes the first international consensus guidelines on resuscitation. The same year, the ARDS Network trial shows that ventilating patients with ARDS at 6 rather than 12 mL/kg of predicted body weight reduces mortality.

history.title: The Civil Contingencies Act
history.detail: The UK Civil Contingencies Act sets out the duties of emergency responders, including the NHS, to assess risk, plan and exercise for emergencies, providing the legal framework for major incident planning.
